source.title: Linguistic Loopholes in LLM Unlearning: From a 174-Language Benchmark to Coverage-Aware Unlearning
source.authors: Tyler Skow; Shravan Chaudhari; Rama Chellappa; Abhay Yadav

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether unlearning transfers across languages and prompt forms, reports residual access through alternative routes, and evaluates a coverage-aware method intended to improve held-out-language forgetting.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the paper’s own unlearning, prompt-route, paraphrase, and COVER results. The cross-lingual acquisition results and cited findings from other studies are not rows. Table 19 reports comparative paraphrase win rates, not absolute restoration to the fine-tuned model.
record.test_reason: The study unlearns TOFU facts in one language with SimNPO, GradDiff and RMU, stopping at matched source-route forgetting. It then measures oracle-normalized residual gold-answer likelihood when the query or answer language, script or paraphrase changes. Its results show forgotten facts staying accessible through other-language routes (versions A and E). It also tests a counter-method, COVER source selection, against that leakage (version F).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that meeting the removal criterion on supervised language routes does not rule out substantial residual access through other query and answer languages, scripts and paraphrases. They suggest the methods suppress syntactic routes rather than semantic pathways. COVER reduces held-out residual by 7.8–27.3% versus uniform selection, with smaller gains on LORELEI. Source weighting gives model-dependent tradeoffs and no generally superior rule.
record.recipe_differences: Tests multilingual unlearning with SimNPO, RMU, and GradDiff and introduces COVER for language-source selection; it does not reproduce the original studies’ attack recipes as a whole.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome depends on query and answer language route, script (native versus Romanized Hindi), paraphrase type, model family, source-language subset, document prompt position, and in some reported evaluations the training order.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuning in one language transfers access broadly on the query side and much less when the answer language changes. Languages that gain the most access also lose the most under unlearning (Spearman about 0.35–0.99).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cross-lingual unlearning transfer tracks cross-lingual acquisition transfer.

record.problems: The main access results use teacher-forced gold-answer likelihood and oracle-normalized measures rather than targeted-knowledge accuracy against chance. Paraphrase results are relative win rates, not absolute recovery rates. Generated-answer leakage is judged by an LLM; the reported human calibration covers 192 facts and gives 81.8% agreement on fact status. Some aggregate results span model/checkpoint groups, and uncertainty is not reported for many table entries.
record.rows_left_out: No cap-driven omissions. Detailed per-language and per-checkpoint results in Appendix C and source-subset grid results in Tables 3 and 22 are not separately extracted; Table 2B aggregate route results and the relevant prompt-form, source-selection, and generation outcomes are retained. Table 19's unranked Format condition is not included because the text states it lacks complete pairwise coverage.

untested.parts: Accuracy versus chance is not measured (likelihood only). Jailbreaks, in-context information and fine-tuning attacks are not tested.
No activation ablation or mechanistic test of blocking versus deletion. The 'syntactic routes' interpretation is inference only.
No jailbreaks or in-context information. The paraphrase effect is not measured in absolute terms (Table 19 is relative).
COVER is not tested against fine-tuning, activation edits, quantization, jailbreaks or paraphrase attacks. It is tested only against held-out-language routes.

missing.what: Table 2B columns: share of other languages ≥90% removed (SimNPO 30.0, GradDiff 71.1, RMU 18.0) and worst-language access left (49.2 / 26.2 / 75.4). The text adds that fewer than 20% of alternative routes reach a→a closure.
English-only forget supervision (K=1) leaves 55.3% full leakage in generated answers across six languages. Best triple gives 19.6%; all-six gives 13.7% with gibberish 16.9% and retain damage 0.130.
RMU bottleneck counts: Russian is the worst alternative language in 27 of 70 checkpoints.
Single-example absolute likelihoods. Script: native Hindi 0.984→0.955 after Romanized unlearning. Paraphrase: post-unlearning likelihood 0.827 versus 0.621.
Costs of COVER and of source weighting. Table 5: gibberish rises (Aya 1.52→4.39). Table 4c: LORELEI retained ΔchrF++ −5.57 for Aya. Table 24: Llama calibrated weights raise gibberish 5.69→18.48.

record.verdict_notes: For rows R2–R9, which are linked to both A and E, the state is scored as recovery (E); for A the direction is the inverse. All access measures are teacher-forced likelihood, not accuracy against chance. Table 2B values are means over 81 monolingual checkpoints per method, and worst-case languages are much higher. Paraphrase rows (Table 19) are relative rankings and cannot establish recovery, so rows R13–R18 stay at cannot_determine. COVER is the study's own method, and its rows compare it with uniform selection rather than with an attack-free reference. F verdicts are therefore based on the absolute residual and leakage that remain.

versions.untested_parts: It measures oracle-normalized answer-likelihood removal and retained performance, not targeted-knowledge accuracy against chance; it does not test every attack type in the claim.
No post-unlearning fine-tuning on unrelated, loosely related, or forgotten-fact examples.
No activation-direction ablation or direct internal test establishing that unlearning blocks access rather than deletes knowledge.
No low-bit quantization of unlearned weights.
Tests cross-language, script, and paraphrase prompt changes; does not test jailbreaks, other attack methods, or in-context information.
Tests COVER’s held-out-language performance, including ordinary native-language routes; does not test resistance to fine-tuning, activation edits, quantization, jailbreaks, or all prompt variations.

relation.reason: Its own results on multilingual unlearning bear on versions A, E and F.

tranche.reason: Residual access remains after unlearning, through other languages, scripts and paraphrases. This argues that version A needs restating, and it bears on E. T3 would also be defensible.

source_check.notes: Table 2B averages 81 monolingual checkpoints (fine-tuned and unlearned in one language) of 3-4B models. COVER's held-out 100R is only derivable (uniform minus reduction: 26.7-44.9 on TOFU). Table 5 leakage averages all six native routes, sources included. Rows R21-R37 compare the study's own method with selection baselines.

statements.problem: none for this study: 81.8 and 63.5 removal leave about 18% and 36% of the acquired gap above the oracle (Table 2B l->l).

statements.correction: Facts fine-tuned in one acquisition language per checkpoint (81 monolingual checkpoints: 27 languages x 3 families), then unlearned in that language. Native other-language removal: 81.8% SimNPO, 63.5% RMU. Models: Tiny Aya Global, Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct. Table 2B has no intervals; 95% intervals appear in Tables 20, 22 and 11.
statements.problem: 81.8/63.5 are right (Table 2B l->l), but Table 2B averages monolingual checkpoints, each fine-tuned and unlearned in one acquisition language, not several. The conditions say '7–8B models', but this study uses Qwen3-4B, Llama-3.2-3B and Tiny Aya Global.

Gives no number or claim naming this study. Of its cited rows, only GradDiff native routes (110.5% removal, below oracle on average) are 'at or below retrain'. Its 3-4B models are missing from the conditions list.

statements.correction: Across monolingual checkpoints, RMU removal is 91.1% with a query-only language change and 63.5% on native routes. Hindi matched-form NLL advantage: 6.05 SimNPO, 8.26 RMU (Table 20, 16 runs, fixed 100 updates).
statements.problem: The numbers are right (RMU 91.1 l->a, 63.5 l->l; Hindi 6.05 and 8.26 NLL), but the facts were not fine-tuned in many languages: Table 2B averages monolingual checkpoints. Table 20 uses a fixed 100-update budget.

statements.correction: TOFU held-out 100R under COVER (derived): Aya 28.5/26.7, Qwen 43.2/40.9, Llama 44.9/42.4 (requests A/B); LUME Qwen 32.13. Llama-3.2-3B reduction: request A +3.80±6.94, request B +7.48±1.94. Tiny Aya Global full leakage 25.57% (Table 5, six native routes).
